conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You’re here because of abdominal pain and nausea again, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s the same pain I always get. I couldn’t keep anything down. I was only home one day last time and it came right back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’re saying this feels like your usual gastroparesis flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. I haven’t had a bowel movement in a week. I’m in so much pain. I just want it to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve reviewed your records. You’ve been through this many times. We’ll start with IV fluids and medications to help with nausea and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But last time, Reglan didn’t help. They switched me to promethazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. We’re not using Reglan this time because it didn’t work before. We’re giving you promethazine and another anti-nausea med as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And can you do something for the pain? It’s really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re giving you tramadol and Tylenol regularly, and dilaudid for breakthrough pain through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My blood pressure was high too when I came in, wasn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your systolic was 253. We’ve increased your nifedipine from 60 to 90 mg daily. That should help bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on that for years. It’s hard to keep it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Pain and stress can make it worse. As your pain improves, your pressure should too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a central line in your neck because your veins are hard to access. It’ll help with giving meds and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s routine. We did a chest X-ray to make sure it’s in the right place. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your kidney function was a bit off when you came in—creatinine was 1.4—but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the diabetes? I’ve had protein in my urine before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. We call it diabetic kidney disease. Your current kidney issue is acute but related to dehydration and the flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it already is. Your creatinine is down to 1.0 today. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One thing—we saw a mild elevation in your white blood cell count, 18.5, but that’s been high before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It’s been high in past records. We call it chronic leukocytosis. No fever or other signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But you did a blood culture, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. One culture showed a small amount of coagulase-negative staph, but it’s likely a contaminant since only one bottle grew it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave one dose of daptomycin just in case, but since you’re not sick and repeat cultures are negative, we’re not continuing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test showed white blood cells, but no bacteria grew. You don’t have symptoms of a UTI, so we’re not treating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve had so many UTIs because of the diverticulum. Shouldn’t I get something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand, but treating without symptoms could lead to resistance. We’ll repeat the urine test as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down—now 10.3. That supports it was stress-related, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s because of the pain and gastroparesis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely. But we’ll suggest your primary doctor look into it further, maybe with a hematology consult.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. You’ve been able to eat soft foods and keep them down. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still nauseous sometimes, but not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the prochlorperazine suppository available. The promethazine by mouth is helping too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted GI. They agree this is a gastroparesis flare. They recommend a gastric emptying study to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had scopes before. Will I need one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, tomorrow. An EGD to check your stomach. It’s mostly to rule out other causes, like ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The EGD is done. Good news—no ulcers or blockages. The stomach looked a bit pale with mild redness, but nothing serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I threw up a lot before the test. Was that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common with severe gastroparesis. They had to intubate you briefly for safety, but you’re okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep advancing your diet. For the gastric emptying study, you’ll need to stop pain meds like tramadol first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the pain comes back if I stop them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why GI may consider other options like domperidone, which isn’t used often but can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Your pain is much better, labs are improved, and you’re eating. We’d like to send you home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue insulin, sertraline, gabapentin, and pantoprazole. Nifedipine is now 90 mg daily. We’re keeping tramadol and promethazine for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the iron pills? They upset my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. Ask your doctor about IV iron—it avoids the stomach and might be easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the port? I keep needing lines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve referred you for evaluation. If you keep getting admitted, a port could make things easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your primary doctor and GI soon. They’ll arrange the gastric study and review your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to get better. I’m tired of being sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. We’ll work with your team to find better long-term solutions. For now, rest and follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. We’re updating your nifedipine and keeping your pain and nausea meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better than I have in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if things worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final note—your blood sugar was high on admission, around 350. Keeping it controlled helps prevent these flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I try, but when I’m sick, it’s hard to eat right or stay on schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. That’s why follow-up is so important. Maybe diabetes education can help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll add that to your referrals. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.
